messages.content: I want to frame the goal for robotic peg insertion. Friction and clearance can change, but those changes are indistinguishable before contact. How should I state the sim-to-real objective?

The objective is to enable safe sim-to-real transfer for robotic peg insertion despite that pre-contact ambiguity. The system should achieve at least 90% insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations using at most 20 real adaptation trials. It must also keep peak contact force below 20 N during both adaptation and deployment, without privileged state observations.
Why is the phrase “indistinguishable before contact” important here?

It rules out treating the friction–clearance combination as something the system can identify from pre-contact information alone. Before contact, the different conditions in question cannot be told apart. The goal does not specify whether contact will reveal enough information to identify them exactly; it states the ambiguity that the transfer must handle.
So should I describe friction and clearance as two separate test conditions?

They are two aspects of the variation, but the success requirement is stated across held-out *friction–clearance combinations*. That wording matters: the target concerns combinations of the two, rather than a claim about friction alone or clearance alone.
What does “held-out” add to the success requirement?

It makes the target about combinations reserved for evaluation, not just combinations encountered while developing or adapting the system. The stated threshold is at least 90% insertion success across those held-out combinations. The goal does not specify the exact scoring or aggregation procedure, so I would not add one.
And the 20-trial limit applies to what, exactly?

It is a limit of **at most 20 real adaptation trials**. That is distinct from the insertion-success percentage and the force constraint. The goal does not further define how an adaptation trial is counted or assign a separate trial allowance to each combination.
Does the trial budget make the force limit less strict during adaptation?

No. The force condition explicitly covers adaptation as well as deployment: peak contact force must remain **below 20 N** in both. The allowance for real adaptation trials is a budget, not an exception to the safety requirement.
Is “below 20 N” meant as an average-force target?
No. It is a **peak contact force** limit, so describing it as an average would change the requirement. “Below 20 N” is also stricter wording than “20 N or below.”
What should I take “without privileged state observations” to mean without assuming a particular sensor setup?

It means the goal cannot depend on access to privileged state information—information supplied as ground truth rather than available to the system under the stated conditions. The node does not name particular permitted sensors or observations, so there is no basis to prescribe or rule out a specific sensing setup here.
Could I say the system knows the friction and clearance before it starts inserting, provided it still meets the numerical targets?

That would conflict with the stated premise that changes in friction and clearance are indistinguishable before contact. Meeting the numerical targets is not the whole goal; the pre-contact ambiguity and the absence of privileged state observations are part of the conditions under which those targets must be met.
Does the goal require perfect insertion once contact has occurred?

No. Its specified performance threshold is at least 90% insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations, not 100%. Contact does not remove the separate requirements concerning the real-trial budget and peak contact force.
How do I keep the performance and safety parts together in one concise formulation?

You could say: “Enable safe sim-to-real transfer for robotic peg insertion when friction and clearance changes are indistinguishable before contact, achieving at least 90% insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations with at most 20 real adaptation trials, while keeping peak contact force below 20 N during adaptation and deployment without privileged state observations.”
That keeps the objective as a target, rather than implying that any experiment has already met it?
Yes. It states what the system is meant to achieve and the conditions under which it must do so. It does not claim that the success rate, trial limit, or force limit has already been demonstrated.

For this peg-insertion goal, I’d like to propose low-force probes for 20-trial Bayesian friction–clearance inference from wrist wrench and proprioception, followed by 18 N upper-confidence-limited impedance insertion. Can you unpack that without treating it as an established result?

Yes. The proposal has two stages. First, use low-force probes and the resulting wrist-wrench and proprioceptive observations to perform Bayesian inference about friction and clearance within a 20-real-trial adaptation budget. Then use an impedance-based insertion approach limited by an 18 N upper-confidence criterion. This is a proposed way to address the pre-contact ambiguity while aiming for the insertion-success and force requirements; it is not a claim that those requirements have already been met.
Why include probes rather than infer the conditions before contact?

The goal says changes in friction and clearance are indistinguishable before contact. Low-force probes would seek information through interaction, using observations that arise when the robot engages with the task. The proposal does not assume that the relevant combination can be identified from pre-contact observations.
Are the probes supposed to be the insertion attempt itself?

The proposal distinguishes low-force probing from the subsequent impedance insertion, but it does not specify the exact motions, whether a probe and an insertion occur within the same trial, or how individual trials are organized. Those details should not be inferred from the two-stage description.
What information is the Bayesian part meant to infer?

It is Bayesian inference about the friction–clearance condition. Calling it Bayesian indicates that uncertainty about those conditions is represented and updated using observations. The proposal does not specify a prior, a likelihood model, or a required level of identification accuracy.
And the observations are specifically wrist wrench and proprioception?

Yes. Those are the named observation sources for the proposed inference. The wording does not call for privileged observations of the true friction or clearance. Nor does it specify particular signals beyond wrist wrench and proprioception.
Does “20-trial Bayesian inference” mean exactly 20 probes?

Not necessarily. The stated goal permits at most 20 real adaptation trials, and the proposal places its inference within that 20-trial scope. It does not say that every trial consists of exactly one probe, that all 20 trials must be used, or that a separate set of 20 trials is available for each held-out friction–clearance combination.
How should I understand “low-force” if the proposal doesn’t assign a probe-force number?

It describes the intent of the probing stage, but it is not a numerical probe-force threshold. The applicable quantitative safety requirement remains that peak contact force stay below 20 N during adaptation as well as deployment. No more specific probe-force value is supplied.
Then what does the 18 N figure govern?

It belongs to the proposed upper-confidence-limited impedance insertion stage. In broad terms, the insertion would be limited according to an upper-confidence assessment at 18 N, rather than simply referring to a measured average force. The proposal does not define how that upper-confidence quantity is computed or enforced.
Why not describe it simply as a 20 N insertion limit?

That would erase a specific feature of the proposal. It names an **18 N** upper-confidence limit for impedance insertion, while the overarching requirement is for **peak contact force below 20 N** during adaptation and deployment. Those are related but different statements: the proposed 18 N criterion is not itself evidence that every actual force peak will remain below 20 N.
Is the upper-confidence limit meant to handle uncertainty in the friction–clearance inference?

That is a reasonable way to read the proposed sequence: infer under uncertainty, then limit insertion using an upper-confidence criterion. But the node does not specify exactly how inferred friction–clearance uncertainty is translated into the 18 N limit. It would be too specific to claim a particular uncertainty calculation or control rule.
What role does impedance insertion play in the statement?

It identifies the proposed insertion approach after probing and inference. The statement does not give impedance gains, a trajectory, a switching rule, or any other controller details. What it does specify is the sequence—low-force probes and Bayesian friction–clearance inference from wrist wrench and proprioception, then 18 N upper-confidence-limited impedance insertion.
Could I present that sequence as guaranteeing the at-least-90% success target?

No. The goal is at least 90% insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations using at most 20 real adaptation trials. This sequence is a proposal directed at that goal, not a demonstrated success rate or a guarantee. The peak-force requirement likewise remains a requirement to satisfy, not an outcome established by naming the proposed limit.

Let me check the wording: “Use up to 20 real adaptation trials of low-force probing, infer friction and clearance from wrist wrench and proprioception with a Bayesian method, and then perform impedance insertion under an 18 N upper-confidence limit.” Is anything important missing?

That captures the proposal’s main elements. To keep its purpose clear, you could add that it addresses friction and clearance changes that cannot be distinguished before contact. If you connect it to the goal, retain the separate targets of at least 90% insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations and peak contact force below 20 N during both adaptation and deployment, without privileged state observations. Those remain targets, not results of the proposed method.
So the proposal should stay specific about its observations and force figure, while leaving unspecified mechanics unspecified?

Exactly. Keep the named ingredients—low-force probes; 20-trial Bayesian friction–clearance inference using wrist wrench and proprioception; and subsequent 18 N upper-confidence-limited impedance insertion. Avoid adding an unprovided probe trajectory, Bayesian model, confidence formula, or claim of measured success or safety.
Can low-force contact probes distinguish friction from clearance using wrist wrench and proprioception within 20 adaptation trials?

That is the key open question for the proposed inference stage. Contact probes could provide observations that are unavailable before contact, but the proposal alone does not establish that wrist wrench and proprioception contain enough information to distinguish friction from clearance—or that they do so within 20 real adaptation trials.
What does “distinguish” require here? Is it enough to notice that something has changed?

Not necessarily. Noticing a change would be weaker than telling whether the observation is attributable to friction, clearance, or some combination of the two. The question asks whether the probes and named observations can separate those possibilities well enough within the trial limit. It does not state a required estimation precision.
Does the fact that the conditions are indistinguishable before contact answer the question either way?

No. Pre-contact indistinguishability explains why information from contact matters; it does not imply that contact observations will distinguish the conditions. Nor does it rule out their becoming distinguishable after contact. That is precisely what the question leaves open.
Why name both wrist wrench and proprioception instead of saying “contact feedback”?

Because the question is specifically about what can be inferred from those two observation sources. “Contact feedback” would be less precise and could suggest observations that have not been named. The issue is whether wrist-wrench and proprioceptive signals, as available during low-force contact probes, suffice for this distinction.
Does having two kinds of observation automatically make friction and clearance identifiable?

No. Multiple observation sources may be informative, but their mere presence does not guarantee that different friction–clearance conditions produce distinguishable observations. The question requires assessing the information they actually provide under the proposed low-force probing and trial constraint.
Could a Bayesian method resolve ambiguity even if the observations look the same?

A Bayesian method can represent and update uncertainty, but it cannot obtain a reliable distinction from observations that provide no distinguishing information. If ambiguity remains, the inference should reflect that uncertainty rather than be described as having identified friction and clearance. Whether the proposed observations reduce ambiguity enough is still unknown.
So this is partly a question about the probes, not just about the inference algorithm?

Yes. The question concerns the combination of low-force contact probes, wrist wrench and proprioception, and the 20-adaptation-trial limit. An inference method cannot be evaluated separately from the information its probes and observations make available. No particular probe motion or Bayesian model is specified here.
What does the 20-trial condition change about how we read the question?

It makes the question about distinguishing the conditions within a finite real-adaptation budget, rather than eventually distinguishing them with unlimited interaction. It does not assert that 20 trials are necessary, sufficient, or all used. It asks whether the distinction can be made within that bound.
Could “within 20 adaptation trials” mean a separate 20 trials for every possible friction–clearance combination?

That allocation is not stated. The question specifies a 20-adaptation-trial bound but does not define a per-combination budget or a trial-allocation scheme. Adding either would make the question more specific than it currently is.
And does “low-force” have a number attached to it in this question?

No numerical probe-force threshold is given. “Low-force” characterizes the contact probes; the broader goal separately requires peak contact force below 20 N during adaptation and deployment. We should not silently turn “low-force” into a different numerical limit.
Suppose the observations suggested several plausible friction–clearance combinations rather than just one. Would that count as distinguishing them?

It would indicate some information, but whether it counts as distinguishing friction from clearance depends on what distinctions remain unresolved. If materially different friction and clearance explanations remain compatible with the observations, a confident claim that the two have been separated would be premature. The question does not specify a quantitative criterion for when the remaining uncertainty is small enough.
Is distinguishing the friction–clearance combination the same as estimating friction and clearance individually?

They are related but not identical claims. One might be able to tell some combinations apart without uniquely determining each component, or retain uncertainty over combinations while learning something about one component. This question specifically asks whether low-force contact probes can distinguish friction from clearance using the named observations within 20 adaptation trials; it does not provide a finer definition of the desired inference output.
Would insertion success by itself settle this identifiability question?

Not by itself. Successful insertion is a performance outcome, while this question asks what can be learned about friction versus clearance from the probes and observations. A system could perform well without uniquely identifying both, or identify them without thereby establishing the separate success and force targets. Those possibilities are conceptual distinctions, not claims about results here.
How should I answer if someone asks, “So can the probes do it or not?”

The faithful answer is that it has not been established in the information given. Low-force contact probing with wrist wrench and proprioception is the proposed route to gaining information after pre-contact ambiguity, but whether it can distinguish friction from clearance within 20 adaptation trials remains the question to resolve.
Can we at least say what would count as a relevant answer, without claiming an experiment has happened?

A relevant answer would address whether the observations available from low-force contact probes separate friction-related variation from clearance-related variation within the 20-trial bound, and it would make clear what uncertainty remains. That describes the evidence needed to answer the question; it does not prescribe an unprovided protocol or report a finding.
Should the later 18 N upper-confidence-limited impedance insertion be part of this question too?

It provides context for the proposal, but this question is narrower: it concerns whether the probing observations can distinguish friction from clearance within the adaptation budget. The later insertion stage does not, on its own, answer whether the inference stage can make that distinction.

Let me restate it: contact may create information absent before contact, but we do not yet know whether low-force probes, wrist wrench, and proprioception can separate friction from clearance in at most 20 adaptation trials.

Yes. That preserves both the motivation and the uncertainty. In particular, it does not treat the proposed Bayesian inference as proof that the necessary information is present, and it keeps the 20-adaptation-trial condition attached to the question.

I have a hypothesis for the probing question: twelve lateral dithers at ≤10 N yield ≤15% median relative error for friction and clearance inferred from wrench–displacement traces. How should we interpret that?

It is a testable hypothesis, not a reported result. It predicts that twelve lateral dithers, each subject to the stated ≤10 N force condition, provide wrench–displacement traces from which friction and clearance can be inferred with ≤15% median relative error. The claim is about estimation accuracy under that probing condition; it does not say the accuracy has been observed.
Does that directly answer whether low-force probes can distinguish friction from clearance?

It offers a specific possible answer. If the predicted error bound holds for both inferred quantities, it would be evidence that the traces carry useful distinguishing information. But the hypothesis itself cannot establish that the two are distinguishable; that remains contingent on whether its prediction holds.
Why specify lateral dithers rather than just saying “contact probes”?

“Lateral dithers” identifies the kind of probe the hypothesis concerns. The earlier question was broader—it asked about low-force contact probes generally—whereas this hypothesis makes a prediction for twelve probes of this particular kind. It does not specify their motion pattern beyond calling them lateral dithers.
Is twelve the number of observations or the number of adaptation trials?

The hypothesis says **twelve dithers**. It does not define how dithers are grouped into real adaptation trials, so twelve should not automatically be restated as twelve trials. That distinction matters when relating the hypothesis to the at-most-20-real-adaptation-trial goal.
But twelve is less than twenty. Can I say the hypothesis fits within the trial budget?

You can say the dither count is twelve and the adaptation budget is at most 20 real trials. Whether performing those twelve dithers fits within that trial budget depends on how a trial is counted and how the dithers are conducted; neither is specified here. The numerical comparison alone does not settle the budget question.
What does the ≤10 N condition apply to?

It qualifies the lateral dithers in the hypothesis: they are specified as ≤10 N probes. The statement does not define the precise force measure used for that bound or extend the 10 N figure to the later insertion stage. It is also distinct from the overarching requirement that peak contact force remain below 20 N during adaptation and deployment.
Could we describe the ≤10 N figure as a measured peak-force result from the probes?
No. Nothing here reports measured probe forces. The ≤10 N figure is part of the hypothesized probing condition, not evidence that any executed probe stayed within it.
And the wrench–displacement traces are what the inference uses?

Yes. The hypothesis ties the predicted friction and clearance estimates to wrench–displacement traces produced by the dithers. That is consistent with discussing wrench and motion-related observations, but the hypothesis does not specify exactly how the traces are processed or what inference model is used.
Does a trace have to identify friction and clearance separately for the hypothesis to hold?

The hypothesis makes an accuracy prediction **for friction and clearance**, not merely for an undifferentiated indication that contact changed. Interpreting it as an answer to the distinction question therefore requires keeping both inferred quantities in view. It does not, however, define a separate mathematical identifiability test.
What should I read into “≤15% median relative error”?

It is a proposed upper bound on a median of relative estimation errors. A median summarizes the middle of a set of errors; it does not mean every estimate has error of 15% or less. The hypothesis does not state the set over which the median is taken, the exact relative-error formula, or how errors for friction and clearance are aggregated.
If the median meets that bound, could some individual errors still be larger?

Yes. A median bound alone does not bound every individual error. That is why the precise statement should remain “≤15% median relative error,” rather than being paraphrased as a per-estimate guarantee.
Should I say the hypothesis predicts a 15% error, or at most 15%?

At most 15% **median relative error**. The symbol ≤ includes 15% itself and values below it. Saying simply “15% error” would lose both the upper-bound meaning and the fact that the metric is a median.
What would relative error be relative to? Would stating that require privileged state observations during insertion?

Assessing an estimation error calls for some comparison value, but the hypothesis does not say how such values would be obtained or when they would be available. That should not be turned into an assumption that the robot receives true friction or clearance as privileged observations during adaptation or deployment. The operational goal remains without privileged state observations.
Does this hypothesis also predict ≥90% insertion success on held-out friction–clearance combinations?

No. Its prediction is narrower: twelve ≤10 N lateral dithers yield ≤15% median relative error for friction and clearance inferred from wrench–displacement traces. Even if that estimation prediction held, it would not by itself establish the separate insertion-success target across held-out combinations.
Or that the later impedance insertion stays under the force limit?

No. The hypothesis concerns the dithers and inference, not the force achieved by a later insertion. The broader requirement still calls for peak contact force below 20 N during both adaptation and deployment; the proposed 18 N upper-confidence-limited impedance insertion is a separate part of the proposal, not a result proved by this hypothesis.
Is it fair to say the hypothesis narrows the open question to a measurable prediction?

Yes. Rather than claiming that low-force contact probes can distinguish friction from clearance in general, it predicts a particular accuracy outcome for friction and clearance inferred from wrench–displacement traces after twelve ≤10 N lateral dithers. Whether that prediction holds—and how those dithers map to the 20-trial adaptation limit—has not been specified as an established finding.
Give me a compact version that keeps all the qualifiers.

“Hypothesis: Twelve ≤10 N lateral dithers yield ≤15% median relative error in friction and clearance inferred from wrench–displacement traces.” That preserves the probe count, force condition, error metric, inferred quantities, and observation source without presenting the prediction as a measured outcome.

To address whether the probes distinguish friction from clearance, I want to plan a check on calibrated held-out pairs: run 12 ≤10 N dithers, fit wrench–displacement posteriors, and compare parameter errors with 15%. Can you walk through exactly what that plan says?

The plan is to use calibrated held-out friction–clearance pairs, perform twelve dithers under the stated ≤10 N condition, fit posteriors from the resulting wrench–displacement information, and compare the errors in the inferred parameters with 15%. It describes a planned evaluation of the probing question, not an evaluation that has already been run.
Why does it say “calibrated held-out pairs”?

“Held-out pairs” keeps the check focused on friction–clearance combinations reserved for evaluation. “Calibrated” indicates that there is a reference against which parameter estimates can be compared. The plan does not say how those references are established or how many pairs there are.
Does using calibrated references mean the robot gets to observe the true friction and clearance while probing?

No. Reference values used to assess parameter error need not be observations available to the robot during adaptation or deployment. The plan says to fit posteriors from wrench–displacement information and then compare errors; it does not grant the robot privileged state observations.
What is actually done during the contact portion?

The specified action is to run **12 dithers at ≤10 N** on the calibrated held-out pairs. The plan does not provide their trajectories, timing, or allocation among pairs, so those details should remain open.
Does that mean twelve dithers on each held-out pair?

The wording does not specify whether the twelve dithers are repeated for each pair or distributed in some other way. It gives a count of twelve dithers for the planned procedure, without stating an allocation rule.
Can I call those twelve dithers twelve real adaptation trials?

Not from this plan alone. A dither is the specified probing action; a real adaptation trial is the unit in the broader trial limit. The plan does not define how dithers map to trials, so the count of twelve cannot automatically be treated as a trial count.
Does ≤10 N establish that the whole peg-insertion process stays below 20 N?

No. The ≤10 N condition is attached to the planned dithers. It does not report measured forces, and it says nothing about peak force during a subsequent insertion. The broader below-20 N peak-contact-force requirement covers both adaptation and deployment.
What does fitting “wrench–displacement posteriors” add after collecting the probes?

It makes the inference step explicit: use the wrench–displacement information from probing to form posterior estimates for the parameters at issue, friction and clearance. The plan does not specify the statistical model, the prior, or whether the posteriors are fitted jointly or separately.
Is the comparison with 15% a comparison of posterior uncertainty, or of estimation error?

The plan says to compare **parameter errors** with 15%. A posterior may express uncertainty, but the stated comparison is about errors in the inferred parameters relative to the calibrated references. The plan does not define an additional threshold for posterior width or confidence.
The earlier hypothesis mentioned median relative error. Should I assume that is exactly the calculation in this plan?

That hypothesis supplies context for why 15% is of interest, but this plan itself only says to compare parameter errors with 15%. It does not explicitly specify the error formula, whether the comparison uses a median, or how errors are combined across held-out pairs. Those details should not be presented as settled parts of this plan.
If the plan doesn’t define the error calculation, can it still address the distinction between friction and clearance?

It is directed at that question because it compares inferred friction and clearance against calibrated references on held-out pairs. The exact strength of any eventual conclusion would depend on how parameter errors are defined and evaluated. For now, this is a plan for obtaining a comparison, not evidence that the distinction has been achieved.
Could I simplify the comparison to one overall error for the friction–clearance pair?

That would add an aggregation choice the plan does not state. “Parameter errors” keeps friction and clearance in view as parameters to assess. The plan does not say whether to report their errors separately, combine them, or apply the 15% comparison in some other precise way.
What can we say about the held-out aspect without inventing a test set?

Only that the pairs used for this planned check are held out and calibrated. Their number, particular friction and clearance values, and selection procedure are not supplied. There is no reported result on them yet.
Does this plan also evaluate the ≥90% insertion-success target?

Not as written. Its specified steps concern dithers, wrench–displacement posteriors, and parameter errors compared with 15%. It does not include an insertion-success measurement, so that separate goal cannot be inferred from this planned comparison.
And it doesn’t test the later 18 N upper-confidence-limited impedance insertion either?

Correct. The described check stops at parameter-error comparison. It does not specify running the impedance-insertion stage or measuring its contact force. Those aspects cannot be treated as evaluated by this plan.
Please give me one faithful sentence for the plan.
“On calibrated held-out friction–clearance pairs, run 12 ≤10 N dithers, fit wrench–displacement posteriors, and compare the inferred parameter errors with 15%.”
And the outcome is still open until that comparison is made?
Yes. The sentence states the planned actions and comparison, not what the errors turn out to be or whether the probes distinguish friction from clearance within the real-adaptation-trial budget.

For the activity, run 12 ≤10 N lateral dithers per calibrated held-out friction–clearance pair, fit wrench–displacement posteriors, and compute median relative errors. Can you spell out what is being done without implying we have results already?

For each calibrated held-out friction–clearance pair, the activity calls for twelve lateral dithers under the ≤10 N condition. The resulting wrench–displacement information is used to fit posteriors, and median relative errors are computed for the inferred parameters. That describes the activity; it does not report the errors or say whether they meet the hypothesis’s ≤15% prediction.
Is “per pair” important in that description?
Yes. The activity specifies **12 dithers per calibrated held-out friction–clearance pair**, not twelve dithers total across all pairs. It does not state how many held-out pairs there are.
And these are specifically lateral dithers?
Yes. “Lateral” is part of the specified probing action. The activity does not give a more detailed motion pattern, so it would be best to keep that description rather than inventing one.
How should I word the force condition?

Say “12 ≤10 N lateral dithers per pair,” or “twelve lateral dithers per pair under a ≤10 N condition.” The activity specifies that bound for the dithers; it does not supply recorded force peaks or extend the 10 N figure to insertion.
Does the activity say the dithers have already stayed at or below 10 N?
No. “Run 12 ≤10 N lateral dithers” specifies how the activity is to be carried out. It is not a report of measured forces from completed dithers.
Where do the posteriors enter?

After the dithers, the activity calls for fitting posteriors using the wrench–displacement information. Those posteriors concern the friction and clearance being inferred. The activity does not specify their statistical form or the fitting procedure.
Should I call them wrench-only posteriors?
No. The specified input is **wrench–displacement** information, so “wrench-only” would omit displacement. The activity does not provide a more detailed account of the signals or their processing.
What are the median relative errors meant to assess?

They assess the inferred friction and clearance parameters against the calibrated held-out pairs. Computing those errors would provide a way to examine the hypothesis that twelve ≤10 N lateral dithers yield ≤15% median relative error for friction and clearance. No computed error values are given here.
Does a median relative error mean every estimate must be within the same percentage?
No. A median is a summary of errors, not a bound on every individual estimate. The activity says to compute median relative errors; it does not state their values or guarantee a per-pair error bound.
Do we know exactly how the medians are calculated across the held-out pairs?

Not from this activity. It names median relative errors but does not specify the relative-error formula, how many pairs contribute, or any additional aggregation rule. Those choices should not be presented as already defined.
Does using calibrated pairs give the robot privileged knowledge of friction and clearance during the dithers?

The activity does not say that. Calibration provides a basis for assessing parameter errors, but it does not imply that the robot receives the reference values while probing or fitting its wrench–displacement posteriors.
How does this relate to the question about distinguishing friction from clearance?

It specifies an activity for assessing that question: gather contact information through the lateral dithers, infer the parameters through wrench–displacement posteriors, and compute errors for friction and clearance. Whether the resulting errors show adequate distinction remains unknown until there are results.
Can I infer that twelve dithers per pair use twelve of the 20 allowed real adaptation trials for that pair?
No. The activity counts dithers per held-out pair, while the goal limits real adaptation trials. It does not define how dithers map to trials or how the trial budget is allocated across pairs.
Does computing the errors also show that insertion succeeds at least 90% of the time?
No. This activity concerns probing, posterior fitting, and parameter-error computation. It does not report insertion attempts or insertion success across held-out friction–clearance combinations.
What is the most faithful compact statement of the activity?

“Run 12 ≤10 N lateral dithers per calibrated held-out friction–clearance pair; fit wrench–displacement posteriors and compute median relative errors.” It states the per-pair probe count, the force condition, the inference step, and the error calculation without asserting an outcome.
We now have the probing figures: across 24 held-out friction–clearance pairs, 12 dithers yielded 11% friction and 13% clearance median relative errors; peak force was 9.7 N. How should I report that?

Report the figures directly: “Across 24 held-out friction–clearance pairs, 12 dithers yielded median relative errors of 11% for friction and 13% for clearance; the reported peak force was 9.7 N.” That keeps the two parameter errors separate and identifies 9.7 N as a peak, not an average.
Are the 11% and 13% figures errors for individual pairs?

No. They are **median relative errors** reported across the 24 held-out pairs: 11% for friction and 13% for clearance. They do not say that every pair had an error of 11% or 13%, or give the error for any particular pair.
Should I combine them into one error number for friction and clearance?
Keep them separate. The evidence reports a friction median relative error of 11% and a clearance median relative error of 13%. It does not provide a combined parameter-error metric.
What exactly does the peak-force figure tell us?

The reported peak force for the dithers was 9.7 N. It is a maximum-force figure for the reported probing activity, not a typical force or an average. It does not describe force during a later insertion.
Can I infer how the errors were distributed among the 24 pairs?
No. The medians summarize the errors, but the evidence gives no per-pair values or distribution. Some individual errors could differ from the medians; their values are not stated.
Does “12 dithers” mean there were only twelve dithers in total across all 24 pairs?

The activity specifies twelve lateral dithers **per calibrated held-out friction–clearance pair**. The evidence reports the resulting figures across 24 held-out pairs. I would retain that per-pair wording when describing the activity, rather than treating twelve as the total across the evaluation.
Do these figures also report insertion success?
No. They report estimation errors for friction and clearance and a peak force for the dithers. No insertion-success percentage is included in this evidence.
What about the number of real adaptation trials used?

The evidence gives a dither count, but not a real-adaptation-trial count or a definition of how dithers map to trials. It would be inaccurate to turn “12 dithers” into a reported number of adaptation trials.
So a careful final wording would leave the measurements as measurements, without adding a conclusion about the whole insertion system?

Yes. State the measured quantities and their scope: **24 held-out pairs, 12 dithers, 11% friction and 13% clearance median relative errors, and 9.7 N peak force**. Those figures do not themselves report deployment force or insertion success.

After the earlier parameter errors met 15%, I want to probe six near-degenerate held-out friction–clearance pairs with 12 ≤10 N dithers and recalculate the parameter errors. What exactly does this activity add?

It adds a check focused on six held-out pairs described as near-degenerate. The activity is to probe those pairs with 12 dithers under the ≤10 N condition, then recalculate the friction and clearance parameter errors. It specifies what to do next; it does not report the recalculated errors or say whether they meet 15%.
Why single out near-degenerate pairs?

The wording focuses attention on pairs that may be especially difficult to distinguish. It does not define a numerical criterion for “near-degenerate,” identify the six pairs, or assert that the probes will distinguish them. The point of recalculating errors is to examine the estimates on that specified set.
Is it accurate to say the earlier 15% result settles the question for these six pairs?

No. The activity is explicitly undertaken *after* the earlier errors met 15%, but it calls for parameter errors to be recalculated on the six near-degenerate held-out pairs. Their errors are not given here, so the earlier threshold result should not be presented as their outcome.
Does “six near-degenerate held-out pairs” tell us whether they were among the previously assessed pairs?
